article.headline: File-Based Plans and Reusable Skills Keep AI Agents Running
article.lede: A developer shares a three-step workflow for long, autonomous AI coding sessions: load a reusable 'skill' that teaches the agent how to coordinate sub-agents, write the resulting plan to a file rather than keeping it inside the active conversation, then execute. The file-externalisation trick is the crux — it keeps the execution context window lean and provides a recoverable checkpoint if the session needs to restart. The poster reports running an agent unattended for four hours using this approach.
article.body:
The workflow centres on **skills.sh**, a package manager for AI agent behaviour. Skills are structured bundles of instructions — markdown files with YAML frontmatter — that tell an agent how to perform a class of task. The *subagent-orchestration* skill referenced here teaches an agent to decompose large jobs, delegate pieces to sub-agents or sequential calls, and synthesise results. The skills CLI, maintained by Vercel Labs, works across Claude Code, Cursor, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot; the specification is intentionally model-agnostic.

The plan-to-file step addresses a structural weakness in conversational AI agents: the *context window*, a finite buffer of text the model can hold at once. Extended planning dialogue — clarifications, revisions, back-and-forth — can exhaust that budget before any execution begins. Writing the plan to a file externalises that state, so the execution session loads only two light artefacts: the skill (for procedural guidance) and the plan file (for task state). The rest of the planning history is discarded without loss.

This also makes long runs recoverable. When context approaches its limit mid-execution, the agent can re-read the plan file to reorient itself, or the user can open a fresh conversation, load the same two files, and resume from a known checkpoint. The plan-as-file pattern is a lightweight form of *persistent memory*: human-readable, diff-able, and independent of any proprietary session format.

The poster notes the workflow was validated using **GLM** — an abbreviation the research sources do not gloss; it most likely refers to the GLM model family from Zhipu AI (THUDM), a competitive open-weight series. If accurate, the four-hour unattended run is a meaningful data point: most autonomous coding agents stall or loop well before that, either from context overflow or cascading errors.

One distinction worth noting: skills differ from *Model Context Protocol* (MCP) servers. MCP exposes typed, API-style interfaces to external tools and data sources — structured calls to databases, browsers, or file systems. Skills are purely prompt-side additions; they add procedural knowledge without modifying the agent's tool surface. The practical rule, as one source puts it: skills for repeatable instruction-heavy workflows, MCP for structured data access.

concepts.definition: The maximum amount of text a language model can process in one session, measured in tokens. When it fills, older content falls away or the session must restart — the central bottleneck in long autonomous agent runs.

A pattern in which one AI agent acts as coordinator, decomposing a large task and directing other agents — or itself in sequential calls — to handle sub-tasks. The orchestrator tracks progress and synthesises results.

A CLI-driven registry of reusable AI agent capabilities, maintained by Vercel Labs. Each skill is a SKILL.md file with structured metadata that agents load on demand. Skills are installed with a single npx command and work across major coding agents.

A standard for connecting AI agents to external tools and data sources via typed, API-style interfaces. Unlike skills — which add prompt-side procedural instructions — MCP servers extend the set of tools an agent can actively call.

repos.summary: The open-source CLI that powers skills.sh, maintained by Vercel Labs. It lets developers install, scope, and publish reusable AI agent skills across Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and GitHub Copilot with a single npx command. Usage telemetry is anonymous and drives the skills.sh installation leaderboard.

article.fact_check: The research sources do not identify which 'GLM' model the poster used; the claim of four-hour autonomous operation is taken at face value and cannot be verified from available sources. One source (newsoro.com) attributes 91.7k GitHub stars to an 'anthropics/skills' repository, but the skills.sh documentation names the underlying CLI repository as 'vercel-labs/skills' — these appear to be distinct projects, and the star count may be conflated with a different repository. Readers should treat that figure with caution.
